description: We are a passionate team of four united by a shared obsession with space exploration, cutting-edge technology, and creative problem-solving. Blending diverse skills in software development, data analysis, and innovative design, we thrive on transforming complex, real-world space data into intuitive, impactful solutions. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aren't just building a project—we are pushing the boundaries of what a small, dedicated team can achieve when curiosity meets execution.
summary:
Radians is a free web tool that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change. Type a star’s name or its RA and Dec, and Radians pulls every NASA SPHEREx exposure of that spot from the IRSA archive, reading only the small patch of pixels it needs. It stacks the exposures from each visit and plays the visits back as a short blink movie. A star that moves jumps from frame to frame; one that brightens or fades flickers.

Two independent finders then point out what moved, appeared or changed, and check each find against Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, CatWISE2020 and known asteroids. Click any star for its 0.75-5 µm spectrum and light curve, or browse the whole sky in all 102 SPHEREx wavelengths on the map.

We tested Radians on the challenge’s five targets. It measures Barnard’s Star moving 10.38″ a year and WISE 0855 moving 8.16″ . In real SPHEREx images with fake sources planted in them, it found all 40 movers at a signal-to-noise of 20.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Radians answers one question for any spot in the sky: did anything change between SPHEREx visits?

You type a name or coordinates, and Radians asks NASA/IPAC IRSA which SPHEREx exposures cover that position. A single SPHEREx file is about 65 MB, so we don’t download any of them. We read only the pixel rows around the target with HTTP byte-range requests. One detector band arrives first, so the first pictures show up in about 9 seconds, and the other five bands follow in the background.

The exposures are stacked visit by visit and played back as a blink movie. A difference view (orange = here now, blue = was here before) and a color-by-time view make motion easy to see. Click any star and you get its 0.75-5 µm spectrum and light curve. Two independent finders flag movers, new sources and brightness changes, and each find is checked against Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, CatWISE2020 and known asteroids. There is also an all-sky map where you can step through all 102 SPHEREx wavelengths.

On the challenge targets, Radians measures Barnard’s Star at 10.38 a year and WISE 0855 at 8.16. RW Aurigae and R Draconis come out as brightness changes, not motion, which is correct. We also planted fake sources in real SPHEREx images: the tracker found all 40 movers at S/N 20 and raised no false alarms when nothing was planted.

BENEFITS

Checking a spot in SPHEREx used to mean Python notebooks and archive queries. With Radians it takes a search box and about ten seconds. There is nothing to install and no account to make. Every view has its own link, so a find can be shared or embedded. Images can be downloaded as FITS for further work or as GIF for sharing.

INTENDED IMPACT

Many of the brown dwarfs and comets we know were found by volunteers flipping through images in projects like Backyard Worlds. SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, more data than professionals can go through alone. We want Radians to do for SPHEREx what WiseView did for WISE: let students, amateurs and researchers check a spot quickly and report what they see. The site is in English and Turkish, and the code is open under the MIT license.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, Astropy, PyVO, NumPy, SciPy) on the server, with our own FITS byte-range reader. Plain JavaScript and Canvas in the browser, plus Aladin Lite (CDS) for the map. A Docker container on Render.com, code on GitHub, about 200 automated tests. No special hardware. We used Claude Code as an AI coding assistant under the team’s direction; the README explains exactly how.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

SPHEREx has no filter wheel. Each exposure sees a spot at a slightly different wavelength, so a plain blink shows “changes” that are only color differences. Radians compares exposures only at matching wavelengths. The same property gives us spectra on the fly, because every exposure is one point of the spectrum. We also measure saturated stars from the light around their cores, and the map has science views for water ice, CO₂ ice and hydrogen gas.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Honesty: candidates are labeled as suggestions to check by eye, false-color images are labeled as false color, and we removed everything that wasn’t SPHEREx data. Speed: first band first, and byte ranges instead of whole files. Reliability: NASA’s archive went down during the weekend, so the five challenge targets are pre-built and open in under a second, and the page explains outages instead of failing silently.
